chapter_theme: Mullai in the rains, second half: the wife waits as the konrai, kodal, kurundham and jasmine bloom and the thunder rolls, refuses the friend's plea that it is not yet the season (118), counts the kodal's whole life passing (119), finds every sight and sound an enemy (121, 122), while the friend urges readiness and reproaches the flowers (112, 116); the last poem turns to the rival women, burned in this life for scorning her (123).

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-clouds and the konrai in bloom fix the rainy season of mullai

comparisons.tenor: the partner he left, as precious as gold

109.reading: The heroine tells her friend, a woman in her own plight, that the clouds which drank the dark sea have come and the konrai has hung out its gold-like strings; the man who left his partner, precious as gold, will not appear, and from now on the two will live apart.
109.nuance: தோன்றுவர் தோன்றார் sets 'he will appear' against 'he will not' in one breath, so line 3 may be her doubt swinging both ways rather than a verdict; என்போல் இகுளை makes the friend another woman left alone.

thinai_evidence.note: the wild jasmine in flower is the mullai blossom of the rains

comparisons.tenor: the wild jasmine's opening, taken as laughter at her grief
the streams running down the hills, taken as tears

110.reading: The heroine says that the greatness of the great is great indeed: when the cool wild jasmine laughed in bloom at her as she grieved with bowed head, the hills, lofty and hard to reach, were moved to pity for one so low and wept in streams, deeply troubled.
110.nuance: Nature splits into mockers and mourners: the small flower laughs, the great hills weep, and that is the 'greatness of the great' of line 1. Line 2 (அரியார் எளியரென்று) is hard; it may instead say that those hard to reach (the hills) came down to her level.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest and the calling sky of the rains are mullai's land and season

111.reading: The heroine tells her friend that the forest has become a festival stage, the glory lilies beckoning like hands, the full sky calling, the bees playing the lute and the peacock that starved through the summer dancing, and asks her to say how one is to stay alive through it.
111.nuance: The whole festival is staged for a return that has not happened, so its gaiety is the threat: உளராகி உய்யும் வகை asks not how to be happy but how to survive.

thinai_evidence.note: sunset, the herdsman's flute and the mullai in the rains

112.reading: The friend tells the heroine that as the sun goes behind the hill and the sweet flute burns in the ear, the man will not leave his word unkept: the kurundham and the mullai have flowered together in the rains, and it is their part now to stand ready to welcome him as a guest.
112.nuance: விதி may be fate as much as duty, so 'our lot is to stand with the guest-feast' can be weary (they wait, ready, once more) rather than confident. The kurundham joined by the mullai is a pair the season shows while the couple are apart, but the poem draws nothing from it, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the herdsmen and their calls belong to the pasture land

113.reading: The heroine tells her friend that even at midnight, when the herdsmen, turning their leaf baskets upside down, call out and drive the herd and the jackal howls, the man who mounted the chariot of spread-maned horses has not appeared.
113.nuance: The herdsmen settle and call at night, the jackal is awake, and only the man with the fast chariot, who could most easily come, does not.

thinai_evidence.note: the kurundham in flower and the rain-clouds are mullai things

114.reading: The heroine speaks to the kurundham: before the many clouds that drank the deep sea could let fall their heavy drops, it blossomed, marked out the season, and so decreed that she should grieve with her bangles slipping.
114.nuance: She blames a tree for the timetable the man set: the blossom is the sign he named, so its coming before him turns his promise into her sentence. The first line (பாத்து, காத்து) is hard, and if வருந்தே is read as a prohibition the tree tells her instead not to grieve. The addressee is the tree.

thinai_evidence.note: the thunder and lightning of the rains, when the chariot should come

115.reading: With the sky roaring like many wide-faced drums and the lightning above like Death with cruel wide eyes, the speaker asks why, for the girl whose long wide eyes stand full of tears and whose soft shoulders are like long bamboo, the chariot has stopped and turned away.
115.nuance: தடங்கண் comes three times: the drum's broad face, Death's eye in the lightning, and her own eye full of tears, so the storm's eyes are set against hers; பணை is drum in line 1 and bamboo in line 3. The speaker is not stated; the third person for the girl suggests the friend speaking to the man or his charioteer.

thinai_evidence.note: the four flowers of the rainy forest are addressed

comparisons.tenor: the white buds, like teeth white as peacock quill

116.reading: The friend reproaches the kurundham, the mullai creeper, the konrai and the wild jasmine: by staying here and putting out flowers and buds white as peacock-quill teeth, they have spread a great pallor, like the ridge-gourd flower, over the bamboo shoulders of the girl with budding breasts and decked, falling hair.
116.nuance: கொன்றாய் is the vocative of konrai and also 'you have killed', so of the four flowers hailed, one is hailed as a killer. இருந்தே, 'staying', sets the plants that stay against the man who went. The addressees are the flowers.

thinai_evidence.note: the thunder of the rains marks mullai's season

117.reading: The heroine tells her flower-garlanded friend that now, when the angry cobra shrinks into its anthill as the rain's thunder rages, the rutting elephant trumpets back at it, and the naagam in the thicket bears its gold beside silver, her soft shoulders have turned pale.
117.nuance: நாகம் is cobra, elephant and the naagam tree in three successive half-lines: the creatures answer the thunder by hiding or by roaring back, while she can only pale. The gold and silver of line 3 (flowers, or the colours of the tree) are unclear.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains have come to the forest

comparisons.tenor: the glory-lily buds opening in the rain

118.reading: The heroine answers her friend: the rains have appeared, the glory-lily buds have opened like the soft finger of a woman, pale herself, trimming a lamp, water has come and the forest has kept its season, so how can she say today that it is not the season.
118.nuance: The friend's consolation, that this rain is not the season he named, is quoted only to be refused. The pallor (பீர்) is put on the lamp-trimmer's finger inside the simile, so the heroine's own paling slips into the flower.

thinai_evidence.note: the white glory lily of the rains runs through its season

comparisons.tenor: the bud lifting like a hood

119.reading: The heroine says the townsfolk talk and she cannot settle whether what they say is fitting; is it fitting, she asks, that the cool white kodal has passed through all its shapes, a ladle, a snake's hood, a finger, a broken bangle, a white parasol, and has withered.
119.nuance: The flower's life is a calendar: from bud to wilting, the whole season the man named has passed while she watched. The first line (உகவும்கள் அன்று) is obscure, so what the townsfolk say is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the konrai in bloom and the hour before sunset

comparisons.tenor: the konrai branches yellowed with flowers

120.reading: The heroine asks whether those who say she has lost her dignity cannot see that the hot sun has turned every branch of the lush konrai to gold, and that before the sun sets on the hill the bees and honey-bees hum the thuttham note without pause.
120.nuance: பீடிலார் may be aimed at her (she has lost her composure) or at the man (he has broken his word); on either reading the bloom and the evening hum are her defence, the season's evidence that excuses grief.

thinai_evidence.note: evening and the dark rain-cloud are mullai's hour and season

121.reading: The heroine says she is one woman, and not one but many foes have taken her for their living, each apart: the anril on the palmyra frond, the evening, the falling rain, the ambal flute, the sea, and, beyond the sea, the dark cloud that rides in blackening.
121.nuance: The list of foes runs across landscapes, the anril and the sea from the shore, the evening, the flute and the cloud from the pasture, so the separation draws enemies from every land. ஆம்பல் may be the evening flute tune or the water lily, and பொருத்தில் is unclear.

thinai_evidence.note: the herders' flute in the flourishing forest

comparisons.tenor: the lightning flashing across the sky

122.reading: The heroine says that as the forest flourishes and the herders' flutes sound, while lightning plays over the gems the boar has dug up as though the sky were laughing, her shameless life seems to break and slip away.
122.nuance: She calls her own life நாண் இல், shameless, because it clings on after the season he named has come; the boar turning up gems is a hill image set in the pasture forest.

thinai_evidence.note: the rival women who scorned the wife are marutham's quarrel, not mullai's waiting

123.reading: The heroine tells her friend that what is done in this life seems to bear its fruit in this life, and those who say it comes in the next do not understand: see how the women with moist hair, who tormented the two of them thinking them weak, have now plainly been burned.
123.nuance: Filed under mullai, the poem has no rain, flower or evening; its matter is the rival women. If 'burned' means their own lovers are now away and the rains scorch them as they scorched her, it stays mullai waiting. Either way a doctrine of deeds and their fruit is turned into a wife's satisfaction.

links.note: In Natrinai 246 the friend sees the golden konrai and the rumbling sky and says this is the season he named, so he will come; in 109 the heroine sees the same konrai under the sea-fed clouds and says he will not appear.
links.teaches: The same golden konrai is read as proof of return by the friend and as proof of desertion by the heroine, which shows that the flower settles nothing by itself: it only fixes the day by which his failure becomes certain.

links.note: In Kural 1222 the parted woman pities the dim evening as a sufferer like herself; in 110 the hills weep in pity for her while the wild jasmine laughs.
links.teaches: The Kural lets the woman lend her grief to one hour of the day, while the quatrain divides the whole landscape into those who mock her and those who mourn with her, so the pathetic projection becomes a judgment on which things are great.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 4: peacocks like dancing women, the konrai in bloom and humming bees make this season the medicine for her pallor, says the friend; 111: the forest as a stage, the bees as lute and the peacock dancing make the heroine ask how to survive.
links.teaches: Set side by side, the two show that the rainy-season pageant had two fixed readings, the friend's cure and the heroine's ordeal, and that the dancing peacock and humming bees are the same evidence in both: what differs is whether one trusts the promise.

links.note: Akananuru 82 makes the hill a stage with bamboo flute, waterfall drum, bee lute and peacock dancer, ending in the heroine alone with tear-filled eyes; 111 rebuilds the stage in the rain-forest with the glory lily's hands, the sky's call and the bee lute.
links.teaches: Moved from the kurinji hill to the mullai forest, the nature-theatre keeps its function of tormenting the lone woman but changes its occasion, from the lover seen by many in secret love to the season of a husband's promised return.

links.note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute, herald of the burning evening, kills like a weapon; 112: at sunset the sweet flute turns hot, and the friend answers that he will not fail and they must stand ready to receive him.
links.teaches: The Kural stops at the killing flute, while the quatrain gives the friend's reply to that very hour, turning the evening's heat into the household's readiness for a guest, so the flute is shown to be a test of trust as well as a pain.

links.note: Kuruntokai 66: the konrai is foolish, blooming on a stray rain before the season he named; 114: the kurundham blooms before the clouds have even shed their drops, and the heroine says it has fixed the season and decreed her grief.
links.teaches: The premature bloom that the Kuruntokai friend waves away as a plant's mistake is, to the heroine of 114, a verdict, which shows that the consolation of untimely rain only works on someone who does not take the flower as the sign itself.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 21: the returning man sees the small mullai buds pointed like the girl's teeth; 116: the friend tells the mullai and its companions that their tooth-white buds have made the girl pale.
links.teaches: The bud that looks like her teeth is a pleasure on the road home and a wound in the waiting house, so the image's sense depends on whether the man is coming: the same likeness that recalls her smile to him drains her colour while he is away.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 10: the thunder roars and the herd bull bellows back at it, and the chariot comes so her body will freshen; 117: the thunder rages, the rutting elephant trumpets back and the cobra hides, and her shoulders pale.
links.teaches: In both the beast answering the thunder marks the height of the rains, and the pair shows that this moment is the hinge of the mullai wait: with the chariot heard it brings her colour back, and without it the same roar is when the pallor sets in.

links.note: Kuruntokai 382: the friend says the rain that opened the mullai is untimely, for if this were the season he would have come; 118: the heroine says the forest has kept its season and rejects the friend's 'it is not the season'.
links.teaches: The Kuruntokai gives the friend's argument from his absence to the season's falseness, and 118 gives the heroine's refusal of it from the forest's evidence, so read together they show the untimely-rain consolation as one move in a dispute the heroine could win.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 11: the kodal putting out clusters like snakes' raised heads announces his swift return; 119: the kodal has gone from ladle to snake's hood to finger, bangle and parasol and has withered.
links.teaches: Kar Narpathu stops the kodal at its snake-hood stage, where it is a promise, while 119 follows the same flower to its withering, so together they turn the glory lily into a clock whose hood marks the hope and whose wilting marks the broken word.

links.note: Kural 1225: the parted woman asks what enmity she did to evening; 121: she says not one foe but many, the anril, the evening, the rain, the flute, the sea and the dark cloud, have made her their living.
links.teaches: The Kural names evening as the single enemy of the parted woman, and the quatrain multiplies the enemies across landscapes, showing that the evening of the Kural was the type of a whole hostile world of sights and sounds, each taking its share of her.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 14: the cool cloud laughs softly as the mullai shows its teeth, and the friend is sure he will come; 122: the sky seems to laugh with its lightning and the heroine's shameless life breaks.
links.teaches: The laughing sky is a good omen in the friend's mouth and mockery in the heroine's, which shows that the same rain-cloud laughter could be heard as welcome or as scorn and that the stock image carried no fixed meaning apart from the speaker.

links.note: Kural 319: harm done to others in the forenoon returns of itself in the afternoon; 123: what is done in this life bears fruit in this life, as the women who tormented us have now been burned.
links.teaches: The Kural's impersonal rule that harm returns soon is here voiced by an injured wife about her rivals, showing how the ethical maxim of quick retribution was taken into akam as a scorned woman's satisfaction rather than a warning to oneself.

links.note: Naladiyar 85 says men who forced themselves on other men's wives in a former birth are born eunuchs in this one; 123 says those who think deeds bear fruit in the next birth do not understand, since the fruit comes here.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar defers the reckoning to a later birth while the quatrain insists on this one, so the pair shows a live disagreement in the didactic age about where retribution is seen, with the love poet choosing the visible, present punishment.

source_issues.issue: Line 3 reads வண்துடுப்பாயப் where the run of -ஆய் forms (பாம்பாய் விரலாய் வளைமுறியாய்) suggests வண்துடுப்பாய்ப்; probably a misprint.
Filed under முல்லை, but the poem has no mullai thing, season or hour; its matter is the rival women, so the inferred thinai is marutham.
